name: Vorozole

lead: Vorozole is an oral aromatase inhibitor that was developed for cancer but dropped after trials showed no survival difference from megestrol acetate. It was never marketed.
Today it is mostly used as a PET tracer for studying aromatase in the brain. It has no studied appearance use.

paras: It competitively blocks the aromatase enzyme, reducing estrogen synthesis.
The sources reviewed do not describe its adverse effects. It is an investigational compound without marketing approval.

lead: Vorozole (developmental code R-76713, tentative brand name Rizivor) is a triazole-based, third-generation nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor that was investigated as an anticancer drug. Clinical development stopped after a comparison with megestrol acetate showed no difference in median survival, and anastrozole, letrozole and exemestane became the standard agents.[1]

It is now best known in research as a radiotracer: carbon-11 labelled vorozole has been used with PET to map aromatase in the human brain.[2] No published trial has tested vorozole for appearance outcomes.

paras: Vorozole is a competitive aromatase inhibitor with very high oral bioavailability, hepatic metabolism and a half-life of about 8 hours.[1] Reviews of aromatase inhibitors place it among third-generation agents studied in breast cancer.[3][4]

PET studies with [11C]vorozole reported a distinctive distribution of aromatase in the human brain.[2] Animal studies used vorozole to examine aromatase effects on male reproductive behaviour in Japanese quail.[5]

Vorozole was tested in breast cancer, where it was compared with megestrol acetate.[1][3] Imaging studies in humans used it as a tracer rather than a treatment.[2] No studies were found testing vorozole for appearance, muscle or body composition.
